item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers are back in Atlanta for Game 4 of the NLDS on Wednesday, needing just one more win to clinch the series. After getting to Chris Sale in Game 3, the Dodgers will face right-hander Tyler Mahle, who has turned heads since being acquired at the trade deadline from the San Francisco Giants.
After batting fifth in the starting lineup for the first time as a Dodger, Shohei Ohtani will once again be hitting in the middle third of the order, this time moving up to the cleanup spot with Teoscar Hernández sliding down to the fifth spot in the order.
Max Muncy makes his first start this series since batting 8th in Game 1 against left-hander Dylan Dodd, this time batting sixth in the lineup with Miguel Rojas getting the day off after dealing with back tightness. The hero of Game 3 on offense, Kiké Hernández, makes his second straight start, this time batting seventh while getting the start at second base. Kyle Tucker once again hits in the 8 spot while Andy Pages rounds things out after a multi-hit performance.
Runs have been hard to come by so far this series, as the Dodgers have plated just 10 combined runs over their first three postseason games, all of which have come via home runs. The main Achilles heel for the Dodgers has been their consistent inability to produce with runners in scoring position, as the team is 0-13 in those situations. The Braves, to their credit, have managed to get one hit with runners in scoring position, albeit across 14 at-bats, and have combined to score just eight runs over the first three games.
The Dodgers have fared well in previous matchups against Mahle, as the right-hander has a combined 3-3 record with a 3.15 ERA. Most of the damage came when Mahle was still with the Cincinnati Reds, and in his most recent start against the Dodgers back when he was with San Francisco, he shut them down over seven shutout innings in a 3-0 Giants win on April 22. Since joining Atlanta, Mahle finished the regular season with a 1.99 ERA and limited the Philadelphia Phillies to just one run in his most recent Wild Card start.

The New York Mets are watching the MLB playoffs from the sidelines after a disappointing 2026 campaign.
However, it’s important to keep tabs on former Mets who are having a profound impact on their new team.
One of those players is reliever Edwin Diaz, who is thriving with the Dodgers so far in the playoffs.
New York Mets fans know Diaz quite well, as he spent six seasons in Queens and was named to two All-Star appearances with the Metropolitans.
More MLB on Heavy: Atlanta Braves Face Major Tyler Mahle Decision After MLB Playoffs
Edwin Diaz Finding Success with Dodgers in MLB Playoffs
Edwin Diaz has had a rocky season after signing a massive contract extension with the Los Angeles Dodgers, but it seems he’s starting to find his footing in recent outings, which included a save in Game Three of the NLDS on Tuesday against the Atlanta Braves.
In the 2026 MLB playoffs, Diaz has allowed zero earned runs over two IP with two strikeouts, one hit allowed, and zero walks.
Looking more broadly, since returning from the IL on September 18, Diaz has turned in seven scoreless innings with 11 strikeouts.
More MLB on Heavy: Kike Hernandez Making MLB History Shouldn’t Surprise Los Angeles Dodgers Fans
Quickly Taking a Look at Edwin Diaz’s Career with the Mets
Edwin Diaz was an All-Star with the New York Mets in 2022 and 2025.
Across 328.1 IP with the Mets, Diaz posted an ERA of 2.93 with 144 saves and 538 strikeouts.
When right (and healthy), Diaz is one of MLB’s most dominant relievers.
It was tough that the Mets had to let go of Edwin Diaz, who had been a staple of their relievers’ corps for several years, but New York was unable to match the Dodgers’ massive offer for the 32-year-old right-hander.

If you have been a Los Angeles Dodgers fan for the past X amount of years, you are aware that Kike Hernandez has been a playoff hero on several occasions.
Well, in his first playoff at-bats this October in Game Three of the NLDS against the Atlanta Braves, Hernandez made his mark known once again with a huge 2-run home run off Chris Sale.
Hernandez’s October heroics feel inevitable at this point, and if the Dodgers are facing a left-handed starter going forward, Kike will almost certainly be in the lineup.
With his fourth-inning home run on Tuesday, Kike Hernandez made a unique piece of MLB history.
“Kiké Hernández is the only player in MLB history to have at least 10.0% of his career homers (reg & post) come in the postseason (min. 100 total homers).”
That is a pretty wild stat, and here are the official percentage numbers for Kike, as relayed by Opta:
Hernández is currently at 11.3% (17/151). The next-highest mark (min. 100 total homers) is 9.4% by Jose Altuve (28/299).
The legend of Kike Hernandez rolls along, and this piece of MLB history shouldn’t surprise any Dodgers fans, who have seen him do this over and over.
Kike Hernandez’s Name Will Be Etched in Dodgers History Forever

Kike Hernandez has seen limited opportunities in the regular season over the past few seasons, but whenever his name is called upon in the MLB playoffs, he doesn’t miss his moment to shine.
It’s pretty remarkable what a playoff hitter he is, and his name has certainly been etched in Dodgers history for his improbable swings.
Under that post by OptaSTATS, there are a few reactions worth noting about Kike:
@The_Parent_Game: “Kiké Hernández spends 162 games making you forget he exists and then 30 seconds in October making you remember. The regular season is just his loading screen.”

@allunsolicited: “Hernandez has 328 plate appearances in the playoffs which is just absurd. .486 slugging in the playoffs vs .402 regular season. One of the more remarkable baseball careers.”

item.content:encoded:
It's October, so of course Dodgers utility man Kiké Hernández is making an impact.
On Tuesday, the Dodgers took back home-field advantage and secured a 2-1 series lead over the Atlanta Braves with their 3-1 win. They are one win away from their third consecutive National League Championship Series appearance and fifth in the last seven seasons.
Hernández's play once again helped the Dodgers to a victory in October, and in the process, he made MLB history.
According to OptaSTATS, Hernández is the only player in MLB history to have at least 10% of his career home runs (regular season and postseason) come in the postseason (minimum 100 total homers).
The 35-year-old is currently at 11.3% (17-out-of-151). OptaSTATS said that the next closest is Houston Astros' Jose Altuve at 9.4%.
The veteran Dodger transforms into a stud once the calendar flips to October. He goes from a steady utility player in the regular season into a postseason monster, boosting his career OPS from .706 up to .831.
“It’s something I take a lot of pride in, but don’t think about it too much,” Hernández said after the game. “Once I’m done playing, I’m going to be someone that looks back and be really proud of my career because of how my career has gone in terms of finding myself each and every year in October.”
Kiké Hernández Takes His Game to Another Level in October
In the past, the longtime Dodger has noted that the intensity and stakes of the postseason sharply elevate his focus and adrenaline compared to the grind of a 162-game regular season.
In 105 postseason games, the Puerto Rican native has hit .272 with a .831 OPS, 17 home runs, 44 RBIs and 81 hits in 298 at-bats.
The Dodgers have scored 10 runs through three games in the NLDS, all of which have come via the long ball. That is the longest streak to start a postseason in MLB history.
Hernández's home run in the fourth inning broke a scoreless tie. It was a two-run shot to left field with Andy Pages on base.
"He's a big-time player," manager Dave Roberts said after the game. "I said earlier, we needed a little bit of that Kiké dust. And he's always prepared. And he loves moments like this. He has a way to lock in. ... It's just one of those things that having him in a lineup in the postseason just adds that extra sort of urgency, that kind of grit that you need."
Two batters later, Freddie Freeman hit a solo shot to right-center against his former team to extend the lead to 3-0.
That was more then enough for ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who was on it on Tuesday night.
The 28-year-old pitched seven great innings, allowing just one run on four hits with 10 strikeouts across 98 pitches.
Yamamoto is 33-0 (including the postseason) when he gets at least three runs of support.
The Dodgers will look to close out the series on Wednesday, with first pitch is at 3 p.m. PT.

Los Angeles Dodgers veteran Kiké Hernández, in yet another stroke of postseason magic, delivered when the team needed him the most.
Kike Hernandez’s moment
After the Dodgers struggled offensively in Game 2, and with a lefty on the mound — an all-world pitcher nonetheless, like Chris Sale — manager Dave Roberts turned to Hernandez to start in Game 3 of the NLDS.
Despite not featuring much during the regular season and producing little when he did, Hernandez hit a two-run home run against Sale.
It opened the scoring for the Dodgers and gave Yoshinobu Yamamoto a cushion. Those two runs would have been enough, with Freddie Freeman’s solo shot serving as insurance.
For Hernandez to deliver once again, now 35 years old, it really does show that there is something about high-stakes moments that bring out the best in Hernandez.
“He’s a big-time player,” Roberts said. “We needed a little bit of that Kiké dust. He’s always prepared and he loves moments like this. … Having him in the lineup in the postseason just adds that extra sort of urgency, that kind of grit that you need.”
How Kike Hernandez always delivers in the postseason
Freeman, who has seen and done a lot in baseball, celebrated how ready Hernandez stays for these kinds of moments.
“I wish there was a recipe for that so we can all take it from him,” Freeman said.
“He’s incredible. He shows up when you need him. He hasn’t had a start in a while, and he goes out there and does what he did. … He’s a Swiss Army knife, and he’s ready to go at all times.”
Hernandez’s home run was the 17th of his postseason career. In fact, he is now the only player in MLB history to have at least 10.0% of his career homers come in the postseason, with at least 100 career home runs.
“That’s probably something that, once I’m done playing, I’m going to look back and be really proud of my career because of how I find myself each and every year in October,” he said.
Until he is done, the Dodgers may need to count on Hernandez one more time, and he will keep himself ready.

Dodgers Manager Dave Roberts Raves About 'Big-Time Player' Kiké Hernández
Kiké Hernández only has one hit in the 2026 MLB playoffs, but it's the biggest hit of the year for the Los Angeles Dodgers.
With Game 3 of the National League Division Series scoreless in the top of the fourth inning and a runner on first base with nobody out, Hernández crushed a changeup from Atlanta Braves ace Chris Sale over the left field wall for a two-run home run, giving the Dodgers a 2-0 lead. Ultimately, that long ball would be enough for Los Angeles to get a 3-1 victory over the Atlanta Braves and take a 2-1 series lead.
"He's a big-time player," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said of Hernández in his postgame press conference on Tuesday night. "I said it earlier, we needed a little bit of that Kiké dust, and he's always prepared, and he loves moments like this. He has a way to lock in. He doubled up on a changeup, and he put a good swing on it and made a couple really nice defensive plays, as well.
"It's just one of those things where having him in a lineup in the postseason just adds that extra sort of urgency and that kind of grit that you need."
The aforementioned home run was the 12th postseason long ball for Hernández in a Dodgers uniform; Hernández, who has extensive experience at every position but catcher (he has even made 11 appearances on the mound), is in his second stint and 10th overall season with the Dodgers (2015-20 and 2023-present).
Two batters after Hernández went deep, first baseman Freddie Freeman did the same, launching a solo home run to right. On the hill, Los Angeles got seven potent innings from right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto, who logged 10 strikeouts and gave up just one run and five baserunners (four hits and one walk). Tanner Scott and Edwin Díaz followed with a scoreless inning of relief apiece.
The 35-year-old Hernández, who traditionally gets lauded for his defensive play and versatility, has been a postseason hero for the Dodgers. With Los Angeles trailing the Toronto Blue Jays 3-2 in the 2025 World Series and trying to extend the series, Hernández turned a game-ending double-play in left field with the tying run in scoring position to force Game 7, which the Dodgers would win in 11 innings.
In 2020, Hernández hit a game-tying home run in the bottom of the sixth inning against the Braves in Game 7 of the NLCS, which the Dodgers went on to win, and he drove in one of the Dodgers' two runs against the San Diego Padres in Game 5 of the 2024 NLDS on a solo home run.
Meanwhile, Hernández blasted three home runs for the Dodgers in a closeout Game 5 victory over the Chicago Cubs in the 2017 NLCS and hit five home runs across 11 postseason games for the Boston Red Sox in 2021.
Hernández, who started at third base for the Dodgers in Game 3 and later moved to left field, was limited to 41 games in the 2026 regular season due to elbow and oblique injuries, respectively.
In all, the Dodgers have scored just 10 runs in the NLDS, but they've held the Braves to seven runs. The Dodgers have the chance to advance to the NL Championship Series in Game 4 on Wednesday afternoon (6 p.m. ET on FS1). Atlanta will send Tyler Mahle to the hill, while Los Angeles counters with Tyler Glasnow.
Should the Dodgers advance, they'd play the winner of the NLDS matchup between the Milwaukee Brewers and Padres, who staved off elimination with a Game 3 win on Tuesday night, in the NLCS.

7 de octubre de 2026 - 9:45 PM
Atlanta - Yoshinobu Yamamoto ponchó a 10 bateadores en siete entradas, Enrique “Kike” Hernández conectó un jonrón de dos carreras y los Dodgers de Los Ángeles vencieron 3-1 a los Braves de Atlanta el martes por la noche, tomando una ventaja de 2-1 en su Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional.
Hernández, quien suele brillar en octubre, sacudió su decimoséptimo cuadrangular en postemporada, quebrando un empate con el miembro del Salón de la Fama de Béisbol Carlos Beltrán.
El boricua ahora está empate con Jim Thome, Aaron Judge y David Ortiz en la lista de jonrones en la postemporada.
Yamamoto dominó el muy esperado duelo contra el as de Atlanta, Chris Sale, quien permitió tres carreras y siete imparables en cinco entradas. Yamamoto, Jugador Más Valioso (MVP) de la Serie Mundial de 2025, concedió solo cuatro hits y una base por bolas, mejorando su récord de postemporada a 8-1.
Los Dodgers pueden ganar la serie —pactada al mejor de cinco juegos— y dar un paso más en su intento de convertirse en el primer equipo de la Liga Nacional en ganar tres títulos consecutivos de Serie Mundial si vencen nuevamente a los Braves el miércoles por la noche en el cuarto partido.
Los Braves esperaban que dar descanso adicional a Sale fuera una fórmula ganadora para este crucial tercer encuentro. Sin embargo, tras dejar a seis corredores en base en las primeras tres entradas, permitió el jonrón de dos carreras de Hernández y un cuadrangular solitario de Freddie Freeman en el cuarto episodio.
Ozzie Albies abrió la novena entrada de Atlanta con un doblete contra el muro entre el jardín derecho y el central ante los lanzamientos de Edwin Díaz, avanzando a tercera base tras un rodado de out de Michael Harris II. Díaz dejó al corredor varado cuando Mauricio Dubón fue puesto out en un elevado de foul al jardín derecho y Mike Yastrzemski fue retirado con un rodado al campocorto Mookie Betts.
Tras una temporada agobiado por lesiones, Díaz se apuntó su primer salvado desde el pasado 14 de agosto, cuando lanzó la novena entrada en blanco contra Milwaukee.
FUe además su primer rescate de postemporada desde el 14 de octubre de 2024, cuanto se apuntó un salvamento por los Mets de Nueva York contra los propios Dodgers en la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional.
Dubón realizó una atrapada saltando sobre la barda del jardín izquierdo para robarle un jonrón a Freeman en la tercera entrada; sin embargo, Freeman logró conectar su cuadrangular una entrada más tarde. El jonrón de Hernández hacia el jardín izquierdo impulsó a Andy Pages, quien había conectado un sencillo. Un out después, Freeman conectó el jonrón número 18 de su carrera en postemporada hacia el jardín derecho, ampliando la ventaja a 3-0.
El mánager de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts, bajó al bateador designado Shohei Ohtani al quinto puesto del orden al bate, debido a que Ohtani registraba un promedio de 3 de 15 en su carrera contra Sale. Ohtani se había ido de 4-0 con dos ponches ante Sale cuando los Dodgers perdieron 1-0 el 26 de agosto en Atlanta. Roberts predijo acertadamente que Ohtani tendría oportunidades con corredores en base al batear en una posición más baja del orden de bateo.
En la primera entrada, con corredores en primera y segunda, Sale ponchó a Ohtani para cerrar el episodio. En la tercera, con dos corredores en base, Ohtani llegó a primera gracias a una interferencia del receptor Drake Baldwin —lo que llenó las bases—, antes de que Miguel Rojas terminara la entrada con un elevado al jardín derecho. Ohtani recibió una base por bolas al abrir la octava entrada frente a Brent Suter, el cuarto lanzador de Atlanta.
Un rodado de Baldwin a primera base, con las bases llenas, impulsó a Dubón —quien había conectado un sencillo— en la quinta entrada, anotando así la única carrera de Atlanta ante Yamamoto.
Rojas abandonó el partido durante un turno al bate en la octava entrada. El segunda base pareció lastimarse la espalda al realizar un swing y fue sustituido por Tommy Edman. Los Dodgers informaron que la lesión consistía en dolor en la zona lumbar.
Tanner Scott sumó dos ponches en una octava entrada sin anotaciones para Los Ángeles.

ATLANTA – Yoshinobu Yamamoto felt trust from Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts when he remained in a crucial NL Division Series game after a stressful fifth inning.
“I’d like to continue living up to the highest expectation,” Yamamoto said through a translator.
Recommended Videos
The right-hander from Japan continues to do more than just meet expectations in the postseason.
Yamamoto struck out 10 in seven brilliant innings, Kiké Hernández hit a two-run homer and the Dodgers beat the Atlanta Braves 3-1 on Tuesday night to take a 2-1 lead in their NL Division Series.
Yamamoto dominated his much-anticipated matchup with Atlanta ace Chris Sale, who allowed three runs and seven hits in five innings. Last year's World Series MVP permitted only four hits and one walk while improving to 8-1 with a 2.14 ERA in 11 career postseason outings, including 10 starts.
His 10 strikeouts were a postseason high for him.
“I was confident and able to control all my pitches today,” Yamamoto said.
The Dodgers can clinch the best-of-five series and take another step toward becoming the first National League team to win three consecutive World Series by beating the Braves again Wednesday night in Game 4.
Atlanta hoped giving Sale extra rest would be a winning formula in the pivotal third game. Instead, after stranding six runners in the first three innings, he gave up the two-run homer to Hernández and a solo shot to former Braves star Freddie Freeman in the fourth.
“He was still touching 100 (mph),” manager Walt Weiss said of Sale. “The stuff was fine. Like I said, maybe the command not perfect. It wasn’t bad. But they did a nice job against him.”
That was all the offensive support Yamamoto and relievers Tanner Scott and Edwin Díaz would need.
Ozzie Albies opened the Atlanta ninth with a double off the right-center wall against Díaz and moved to third on Michael Harris II's groundout. Díaz stranded the runner and earned a save when Mauricio Dubón fouled out to right field and Mike Yastrzemski grounded out to shortstop Mookie Betts.
A homer for the boo birds
Freeman said he didn't mind being booed by Atlanta fans in the sellout crowd of 42,420.
“I’ve got a gray uniform on,” Freeman said. “I expect boos. It’s OK. ... It’s all love. I still love everybody here and I’m looking forward to tomorrow.”
Dubón made a leaping catch over the left-field wall to rob Freeman of a home run in the third. Freeman wouldn't be denied an inning later. Hernández's homer to left drove in Andy Pages, who singled. One out later, Freeman pulled his 18th career postseason homer to right field for a 3-0 lead.
Lineup change
Roberts moved designated hitter Shohei Ohtani down to No. 5 in the lineup because Ohtani was 3 for 15 in his career against Sale. Ohtani went 0 for 4 with two strikeouts against Sale when the Dodgers lost 1-0 on Aug. 26 in Atlanta.
Roberts correctly predicted Ohtani would have opportunities with runners on base hitting lower in the order.
With runners on first and second in the first, Sale struck out Ohtani to end the inning. With two runners on base in the third, Ohtani reached on catcher's interference by Drake Baldwin to load the bases before Miguel Rojas ended the inning with a flyball to right field. Ohtani walked to lead off the eighth against Brent Suter, Atlanta's fourth pitcher.
Baldwin's bases-loaded grounder to first base drove in Dubón, who singled, in the fifth for Atlanta's only run.
Injury report
Rojas left during an at-bat in the eighth. The second baseman appeared to injure his back on a swing and was replaced by Tommy Edman. The Dodgers announced the injury as lower back pain.
Roberts said Rojas probably won't start on Wednesday and his availability off the bench will be determined before the game.
“I give him credit for conceding that at-bat,” Roberts said.
Weiss made a late change, moving Ronald Acuña Jr. from right field to designated hitter. Weiss said Acuña jammed his knee on a slide in Game 2. Acuña remained in the game but the knee was sore on Tuesday, leading to the lineup change.
Milestone win for Roberts
Roberts now has 71 career postseason wins, tying Tony La Russa for second-most in major league history. Joe Torre is first with 84.
Up next
Braves right-hander Tyler Mahle is expected to face Dodgers right-hander Tyler Glasnow in Game 4 on Wednesday night. Mahle said Tuesday an abdominal pull is now a “non-issue.” He felt the pull before allowing one run in seven innings of a 4-3 loss to Philadelphia in 10 innings during the NL Wild Card Series last week.

And yet, in a 3-1 win, it was the home run ball, paired with a masterful performance on the mound from right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto, that secured the victory.
The Dodgers pulled ahead to a 2-1 lead in the best-of-five series.
The Dodgers tried to score in other ways, putting on six baserunners in the first three innings of the game. But it didn’t work.
They failed to take advantage of some luck and poor defense from the Braves in the first inning, as Mookie Betts beat out a soft ground ball up the first base line and Teoscar Hernández reached on a fielding error by Braves shortstop Ha-Seong Kim.
Yoshinobu gives up four hits and strikes out 10 and Kiké Hernández hits a two-run home run to power the Dodgers to victory in Game 3 of the NLDS.
The lineup shuffling manager Dave Roberts did against Sale had superstar Shohei Ohtani, batting fifth, walking up to the plate with two outs and runners on first and second. His over-anxious approach at the plate so far this postseason followed him into the at-bat. And he struck out whiffing on a slider in the opposite batter’s box.
The next inning, Kyle Tucker hit a two-out single into left, baited Sale into picking over to first base twice, and then stole second. But he was stranded there, as Kiké Hernández went down swinging. All six of the Dodgers’ outs in the first two innings came via the strikeout.
In the third, the Dodgers loaded the bases. Mookie Betts started the effort with a double through the left side of the infield. And it looked for a moment as if Freddie Freeman had capitalized on the opportunity with a runner in scoring position.
He stayed back on a fastball and crushed it to deep left field, on a trajectory to just clear the short fence. But Braves left fielder Mauricio Dubón made a leaping catch, holding into the ball as he slammed into the wall.
Undeterred, the Dodgers kept putting runners on base. With two outs, Will Smith stayed through a slider to single. Ohtani clipped Braves catcher Drake Baldwin’s mitt and was awarded first base for catcher’s interference. Then Miguel Rojas, who’d exit the game in the eighth inning mid-at-bat with what the Dodgers called low back pain, hit a line drive that found leather to end the inning.
So, back to the long ball.
Perennial postseason hero Kiké Hernández delivered the first blow. With Andy Pages on first, after his first hit of the series, Hernández launched a changeup into the left-field stands. Then, two batters later, Freeman turned on an inside sinker and sent it over the right-field fence — where Dubón had no chance to track it down.
Game 3 was billed as a matchup between aces: Sale, whom the Braves tabbed for Tuesday because of his workload in their wild-card series, and Yamamoto, whom the Dodgers partially held back for the first two games with the NLCS in mind.
Yamamoto held up his end of the bargain, limiting the Braves to four hits and one run in seven innings.
He retired 10 of the first 11 batters he faced. The only baserunner in that time, Michael Harris II, bunted for a single. Yamamoto crashed hard, slipping on the slick grass as he tried to pivot but still managing to make a throw to first from the ground.
Shohei Ohtani is batting fifth in the lineup against Braves ace Chris Sale in Game 3 of the NLDS. He hasn’t hit fifth or lower in a starting lineup since 2020 with the Angels.
He only wavered in the fifth, loading the bases with a pair of singles and a four-pitch walk. The Braves’ batting order turned over, and Yamamoto got Baldwin to ground out to first, but that allowed a run. Then he induced Ronald Acuña Jr. to ground out to second to escape the jam. Rojas ranged to his left to field the ball and made an on-target throw even as he slipped on the grass in shallow right field.
Yamamoto didn’t allow another baserunner.
Left-handed reliever Tanner Scott served as the Dodgers’ setup man, throwing a hitless eighth. And right-hander Edwin Díaz came in for his first save opportunity since Aug. 14 against the Brewers.
He gave up a double off the wall to Ozzie Albies to open the inning but retired the next three batters.

ATLANTA -- After three scoreless innings of tight pitching at Truist Park, the Dodgers broke NLDS Game 3 open with a pair of fourth-inning home runs against Braves ace Chris Sale.
The two-homer frame marks only the second time in Chris Sale’s postseason career that he has allowed multiple home runs in a single start. It happened previously on April 1, 2023, when Sale was with the Red Sox.
Kiké Hernández provided the initial spark, crushing a 406-foot two-run shot to left field to break the scoreless tie and put Los Angeles on the board. Just two batters later, Freddie Freeman delivered a dose of sweet-swinging revenge. After having a potential home run robbed by left fielder Mauricio Dubón in the third inning, Freeman made sure there was no doubt on his next trip to the plate, launching a solo shot deep into right-center field to extend the lead to 3-0.
The pair of big flies extended a historic postseason trend for Los Angeles: All 10 of the Dodgers' runs scored so far this postseason have come via the home run, marking the longest streak to start a postseason in MLB history.
Both home runs also provided individual milestones in the October record books.
For Hernández, the blast marked his first home run of the 2026 postseason and the 17th of his career, continuing his reputation as a clutch playoff hitter -- "October Kiké," if you will. He went 1-for-4 with two strikeouts.
“Experience helps a lot," Hernández said postgame on FOX. "Coming through in big moments helps a lot. Understanding that you can do it in the bigger moments. This is what I grew up dreaming about, playing October baseball. ... I’ve been lucky enough to play for two organizations that have put me there, and given me opportunities, and I’ve made the best of them.”
Freeman’s solo shot was his second of the 2026 postseason and the 18th of his playoff career, tying him with seven others for 10th on the all-time postseason home run list, including teammate Max Muncy, who got there in Game 2 of the NLDS. Freeman went 1-for-4 with a walk and a strikeout.
"It’s an extremely hard at-bat for a lefty," Freeman said of facing Sale on FOX. "I always say, against him, you’ve got to be prepared to die. Really, that’s the mindset. If you pull off of him, you have no chance. He’s throwing behind you and if he hits you in the ear, you’ve got to be ok with it. That’s my mentality, and thankfully I was able to get a good swing on some balls tonight.”

Freddie Freeman and Kiké Hernández continue to add to their postseason résumés.
An inning after Freeman was denied an opposite-field home run over the left field wall at Truist Park by Mauricio Dubón, he thought he might try hitting one right.
But Hernandez needed to show off his bat first.
The two got the Dodgers on the board, to give them a 3-0 lead in the fourth inning of the NLDS, by hitting home runs over the walls in left and right field.
Hernández saw an 89 MPH changeup come his way by Braves starting pitcher Chris Sale and sent it 406 feet out of the park for a two-run homer. One batter later, Freeman obliterated a 96 MPH sinker and sent it screaming off the bat at 103 MPH for 399 feet.
Sale managed to get out of the inning in the following at-bat, but at first glance, it looked he was going to gve up another homer.
Teoscar Hernández just came short of Sale’s slider out of the park, after hard-hitting Sale at 108 MPH.
Both Freeman and Hernandez, continue to show why they are dominant in October, as both of them have had playoff heroics.
Freeman has a career batting average of .268 with 82 hits, 17 home runs, and 40 RBI through 81 postseason games.
Kiké Hernández has a career average of .272 with 80 hits and 16 home runs, with 42 RBIs in the postseason.
The combination of Hernández and Freeman came on the same day; manager Dave Roberts made a surprising decision to bump four-time MVP Shohei Ohtani down to the fifth hole in the Dodgers lineup and have Freeman hitting second, behind Mookie Betts, while Hernández was hitting ninth.
So far, his decision is paying off as Los Angeles holds a 3-1 lead against the Braves.

item.content:encoded:
Despite an injury-plagued season for Shohei Ohtani, 2026 has been a really good year for the Los Angeles Dodgers. After signing Kyle Tucker in the offseason and trading for Tarik Skubal at the trade deadline, they loaded up their roster yet again en route to the second best record in all of baseball. But with the Dodgers painted as the “bad guy” over the last few seasons, the team may ultimately have a major say in the potential 2027 lockout.
With a total luxury tax payroll of over $420 million, the Dodgers spent more money than the four lowest-spending in the league combined. Not only has that drawn the ire from opposing fan bases, but it puts the Dodgers into the spotlight regarding the Major League Baseball Collective Bargaining Agreement negotiations. The owners are eyeing a salary cap to curb spending. But that’s a concept that players like Kiké Hernández refuse to entertain.
As reported by Andy McCullough of The Athletic, the Dodgers clubhouse has not been immune to feeling the burn of that ire and the pressure of a potential lockout next season. But that doesn’t mean that the players are getting desperate. Hernández even acknowledged that the guys in the Dodgers clubhouse know exactly how the game is played on and off the field.
“Whenever things like a CBA come around, there always has to be a bad guy in order for the opposition to want to change things,” Hernández told The Athletic. “And we just happen to be the ones to blame, at this point. Obviously, probably well-deserved, because of the way the last couple of years have gone. Especially with the spending.”
Obviously that spending has paid off for the Dodgers, but does it put them at an unfair competitive advantage?
Kiké Hernández feels like the Dodgers are doing things the right way
Outside of the COVID-shortened season in 2020, the Dodgers have not had a payroll under $200 million since 2018. But as we’ve seen with teams like the New York Mets, spending money doesn’t always equate to a World Series title, or even fielding winning teams that can make it to the postseason.
But with the opportunity to win their third consecutive World Series and their fourth in seven seasons, the Dodgers have spent their money the right way. They’ve made the majority of their acquisitions count and they haven’t taken on too many bad contracts in recent years. The team even boasts a strong minor league system with affordable players like Josue De Paula.
Granted, the deferred money with Ohtani’s contract is the mother of all workarounds, but they still played by the rules when finalizing that deal. That is something that Hernández feels like every team should be doing.
“If you own a team, it would make sense that you’re trying to make that team the best possible, in order to win,” added Hernández. “Because if not, you’re just treating the team as a stock. And why would you want to compete against other people if you’re just trying to make money? Sell the team to somebody who actually wants to compete and win.”
Obviously professional sports are a business. A multi-billion dollar business at that. But at the heart of that business is a game. As Hernández describes it, the Dodgers are just out to win that game and collect another ring. Other teams may lack the budget to stretch their payroll like the Dodgers, but who is most to blame for that?
As of this season, there are just two MLB owners who don’t have a net worth of at least a billion dollars. Bob Castellini of the Cincinnati Reds has $400 million to his name and Dick Monfort Colorado Rockies has a net worth of $700 million. So there is plenty of money to go around baseball. It just comes down to who is willing to spend it in order to win. And winning is something that the players don’t want to negotiate on.

ATLANTA, GA — Dave Roberts spent Monday weighing changes on both sides of the ball before Game 3 in Atlanta.
The Dodgers manager said he is considering lineup tweaks against Chris Sale, including the possibility of moving Shohei Ohtani lower in the order. He also made it clear that Edwin Díaz has worked his way back into serious ninth-inning consideration after his sharp outing in Game 2.
With the NLDS tied 1-1, Roberts sounded open to adjusting quickly.
Díaz Could Close
“I think that we’ve built him up, regained the confidence in him and himself,” Roberts said of Díaz. “I think that it’s certainly a viable option for tomorrow night. I feel very confident with him finishing a game.”
Roberts said Díaz’s most recent outing was about as good as he has seen from him.
“That last outing was as good as we’ve seen him throw, and it’s hard to imagine throwing any better,” Roberts said. “He’s put himself in a position to be the closer.
“In October, I don’t pay too much attention to the long sample of a season in a lot of cases, because in October things happen quickly and you’ve got to be willing to read and react.”
Roberts also praised the way Díaz handled a difficult season.
“Character,” he said. “That’s the main thing. When things aren’t going the best and how players respond, that’s telling.
“The way he stayed the course, dealt with the injuries, went to OKC on a longer rehab to work things out and then took on whatever role we had for him says a lot about him.”
Lineup Changes Are on the Table
Roberts also acknowledged that the Dodgers could look different against Sale.
“I am considering it,” he said. “I think that’s a very fair question. I have to be mindful of it being two games, and then within those two games, what have I seen? Are we seeing good at-bats?”
He pointed to Will Smith as someone whose results have not matched the quality of his plate appearances.
“I think Will Smith is taking good at-bats, just missing some pitches, taking good swings, not chasing much,” Roberts said. “Versus other people maybe expanding, trying to do too much.
“Those are things that you’re trying to make bets on. Then you’re looking at tomorrow with Sale, the history, recency, how guys are prepared and will prepare for Sale. So yeah, I’m thinking through that, and there are possible changes.”
Roberts listed Kiké Hernández, Miguel Rojas and Max Muncy among the options he could work into the lineup.
“At the end of the day, our guys are our guys,” he said. “I can tweak a lineup. I can insert, take out a player or two, but we still have to go out there and play, execute and take good at-bats.”
Moving Ohtani Is Possible
Roberts said he would consider moving Ohtani further down in the order if he believes it helps the team.
“I would,” he said. “I think moving him from one to two, but going further than that, I’m open to it.
“If I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. At the end of the day, every conversation I’ve had with him is whatever is best for the team, he’s all in on. I know that undoubtedly.”
Roberts thinks some of Ohtani’s recent issues have come from trying to do too much.
“I think there’s a little bit of trying to do too much,” he said. “Everything orbits around Shohei in the sense of his talent, and the Braves are going to enter with caution. They’re going to continue to expand as long as we keep giving that to them.
“Until we show some discipline, they’re going to continue to use that playbook.”
He also said Ohtani may be pressing for power.
“Hitting homers, slugging is so much a part of his hallmark in the batter’s box,” Roberts said. “He’s very in tune with what’s being said, what he hasn’t done.
“But that base hit the other way yesterday, that’s production. Against a guy like Chris Sale, that gives you a chance. Trying to chase slug tomorrow night might not be the right plan given the starter.”
Roberts Still Believes in Pages
Andy Pages has also struggled, but Roberts said he plans to keep giving him chances.
“I’m going to continue to give Andy leash,” Roberts said. “I believe in him. I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re going to need him to be an active part of our team.
“This is, for me, given how he has come into the postseason, too small of a sample. He has taken two walks. Tomorrow is not going to be the end-all, be-all because Sale is a tough matchup, but I still want to see good at-bats.”
Roberts believes the main issue is pressing.
“I think there’s trying to do too much,” he said. “When he came back, he was swinging the bat really well, had success, and now I think there’s a little bit of trying too much.”
Freeman Looks Healthier
One hitter Roberts feels especially good about is Freddie Freeman.
“I think he’s gotten into his legs a lot more,” Roberts said. “He’s moving balls in the hitting zone forward. He’s as healthy as he’s been in quite some time. I think the mechanics are sound.”
Roberts credited the five-day break with helping Freeman get his knee into better shape.
“The week off was really crucial for him,” he said. “Being able to manage that with the five days off got him back to health to be able to work through some things without having to perform in a game setting.”
Sale vs. Yamamoto
Roberts expects Sale to attack the Dodgers much the same way he did when Atlanta faced them in August.
“The fastball just sort of bullied us at the top of the zone,” Roberts said. “There was some chase down below, and with the lefties, throwing more two-seamers to keep us honest in and then expand away.”
Still, Roberts believes the Dodgers are in a better offensive place than they were then.
“I do think we are in a different spot,” he said. “The stakes are certainly higher. There is familiarity on both sides. I think we’ll see better at-bats.
“Chris is going to be tough regardless. We know that. We know we’re going to be in for a dogfight, but I just don’t see him bullying us like he did his last start.”
And Roberts feels good about the pitcher the Dodgers will send out against him.
“There should be a lot of talk about Chris Sale, but our guy’s pretty dang good,” Roberts said. “He’s been a very good pitcher in the postseason, so we feel very good about that.
“I think both pitchers are going to pitch well. It’s kind of who grinds out at-bats best.”

LOS ANGELES --Enrique Hernándezis probably headed to the injured list because of a strained left oblique only two days into his season debut for the Los Angeles Dodgers.
The 34-year-old utility man homered in his first at-bat Tuesday night, then doubled in his second before leaving a 15-6 win over the Colorado Rockies after his at-bat in the fourth inning.
"It's not a season-ending thing, so that's something to be hopeful with," manager Dave Roberts said after the game. "But yeah, it's just a bummer."
Hernández was off to a hot start after sitting out the first 53 games of the season while rehabbing from left elbow surgery during the offseason. He went 4-for-4 with two doubles and a homer in his first two games. Fans gave him a standing ovation when he was introduced Monday and cheered him loudly again Tuesday.
A chastened Hernández acknowledged he tweaked his oblique during batting practice Monday, shortly before telling reporters that he was pain-free.
"I was embarrassed because it didn't even happen in the game," he said. "I thought it was just weird tightness. Never done an oblique before, so I didn't really know what I was feeling. Compared to some of the things I've played through in the past, it was nothing."
He received treatment before Tuesday's game and believed he could start and bat ninth in the lineup.
"The homer swing felt awful. The next at-bat I went out there, I swung and missed on the first pitch and didn't feel great," Hernández said. "After that I went into survival mode."
Roberts talked to him in the dugout during the game, urging him to keep his head up.
"Honestly, at that point I was kind of not there, so I'm not necessarily sure everything that he said to me," Hernández said. "I feel pretty defeated right now. Hopefully, we get somewhat good news tomorrow."
Initially, he said he felt pain only when he was swinging.
"That's kind of why I thought I could play," Hernández said. "When I hit the double, it didn't just hurt to swing, it also hurt to run, so I knew that it was time to stop."
Teammate Mookie Betts sustained a right oblique strain in early April while running the bases. The 33-year-old shortstop missed 36 days before being activated on May 11.
"It sucks," Betts said. "We saw as soon as he came he brought life to us, but we'll just see how the rehab and whatnot goes. He'll be back."

The Los Angeles Dodgers have faced two bullpen games to kick off their National League Division Series battle with the Atlanta Braves.
On Tuesday, things will get much more difficult.
The Dodgers are going up against 10-time All-Star and former Cy Young award winner Chris Sale. The left-hander is coming off a regular season in which he had a 2.16 ERA and 200 strikeouts over 162.2 innings. He then allowed three runs over 6.1 innings in his wild-card Game 1 start, and pitched 1.1 scoreless innings to close out Game 3.
The Dodgers know what they're up against with Sale, one of baseball's best pitchers.
"Chris is going to be tough," Roberts said. "We know we're going to be in for a dogfight."
The difficult lefty matchup also has manager Dave Roberts considering some lineup changes.
“I think so," Roberts said. "I am considering it. I think that’s a very fair question. I think that I have to be mindful of — it’s two games, and then with the two games, what have I seen?”
Roberts mentioned Enrique Hernandez and Miguel Rojas as potential options to be in the lineup. The only Dodgers with any semblance of success against Sale in their careers are Mookie Betts (7-for-18) and Freddie Freeman (5-for-16).
The Dodgers have been especially reliant on the home run this series, with all seven of their runs coming via the long ball.
In Sunday's Game 2, they went 0-for-8 with runners in scoring position.
Sale faced the Dodgers on Aug. 27, firing a complete-game shutout with 11 strikeouts and just five hits allowed.
Dave Roberts Considering Moving Shohei Ohtani Down in the Lineup
The Dodgers have plenty of players struggling in the lineup, including Will Smith (0-for-8), Andy Pages (0-for-7) and Tommy Edman (0-for-5).
At the top of the lineup, however, is Shohei Ohtani, who is 2-for-8 with two singles and two strikeouts. He's looked far from his usual self.
"I think there's, like we've talked about, he's not 100%," Roberts said on Monday. "But at the end of the day, he can still do a better job of staying in the strike zone. ... I think that's something that — it's hard to have success when you're out of the zone. ... And Shohei understands, any hitter understands that. So I think that's the thing is — then the question is how do we get him into it? I think there's a little bit of trying to do too much. I think that's a piece."
Roberts said he's open to moving Ohtani down in the lineup, especially with the tough left-hander on the mound.
However, he wouldn't commit to anything on Monday.
"Going further than [No. 2]? I'm open to it," Roberts said. "It's something that, if I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. And at the end of the day, every conversation I've had with him is, whatever is best for the team, he's all in on.”
For what it's worth, Ohtani is 3-for-15 against Sale in his career with five strikeouts.
"At the end of the day, our guys are our guys," Roberts said. "And, yeah, I can tweak a lineup. I can kind of insert, take out a player or two. But at the end of the day we still have got to go out there and play and execute and take good at-bats."

Move Shohei Ohtani down in the Dodgers’ lineup? Dave Roberts is ‘open’ to it
- Click here to listen to this article
ATLANTA — As the Dodgers mull potential lineup changes for Game 3 of the National League Division Series, manager Dave Roberts said he is “open” to moving Shohei Ohtani lower in the batting order.
In his three seasons with the Dodgers, Ohtani has batted first or second in every game he has started. However, as he has admitted he is trying to “manage” in the aftermath of knee and arm injuries, and as Roberts has acknowledged Ohtani is “not 100%,” the lack of success could compel the manager to replace him at the top of the lineup with a more productive hitter at some point.
“I would,” Roberts said Monday. “I would. I think it’s something that, you know, I think moving him from 1 to 2 — but going further than that? I’m open to it.
“And it’s something that if I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. And at the end of the day every conversation I’ve had with him is whatever’s best for the team, he’s all-in on. So I know that undoubtedly.”
It would be strange for the Dodgers to bench Shohei Ohtani, but it’s clear that pretending he’s healthy enough to provide meaningful at-bats isn’t helping.
The Dodgers are batting .215 through the first two games of the NLDS, with the Atlanta Braves scheduled to pitch left-handed ace Chris Sale in Game 3 on Tuesday. If the Dodgers lose, they would need to win back-to-back elimination games to advance beyond this series.
Roberts said the lineup changes he would consider include starting Kiké Hernández and Miguel Rojas, both of whom hit well against left-handers. That could mean infielders Max Muncy (0 for 7 against Sale, with five strikeouts) and Tommy Edman (0 for 11 against Sale) might not start.
Center fielder Andy Pages, who batted so poorly last October he was benched for the final three games of the World Series, is hitless in seven at-bats in this series, with four strikeouts.
“I’m gonna continue to give Andy leash,” Roberts said. “I believe in him. I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re gonna need him to be an active part of our team.
Roberts said he did not envision benching catcher Will Smith, who is 0 for 8 in the series. The Dodgers’ backup catcher, Hunter Feduccia, is a career .205 hitter with no postseason experience.
But, even with the Dodgers’ star-studded lineup, the spotlight shines brightest on Ohtani.
Ohtani has not homered since Aug. 18. He hit .157 between then and the end of the regular season, striking out in 41% of his at-bats. In this series, he has two hits and two strikeouts in eight at-bats, and his inability to refrain from swinging at pitches outside the strike zone has become a glaring weakness.
“He’s not 100%,” Roberts said. “But, at the end of the day, he can still do a better job of staying in the strike zone.”
Ohtani hasn’t given the Braves a reason to challenge him within the strike zone.
“Everything orbits around Shohei, in the sense of his talent,” Roberts said. “And the Braves are going to enter with caution. And, so, knowing that, they’re going to continue to expand as long as we keep giving that to them. So until we show some discipline, they’re going to continue to kind of use that playbook.”

ATLANTA –– The Dodgers don’t want to overreact to a two-game sample size.
But, with elimination all of a sudden just two games away, they don’t want to wait too long to make changes either.
That’s what dynamic manager Dave Roberts was grappling with on Monday, as the Dodgers gathered at Truist Park in Atlanta ahead of Game 3 of their National League Division Series against the Braves.
A daunting challenge awaits on Tuesday night, when the club will face Braves ace Chris Sale for the first time since he threw a complete-game shutout against them in August.
Thus, even though the team’s quest for a World Series three-peat just began, potential lineup changes were already under consideration.
And even superstar Shohei Ohtani might not be immune.
“I am considering [changes],” Roberts said. “I think that’s a very fair question.”
That didn’t mean Roberts was ready to commit to any significant alterations ahead of a pivotal Game 3, with the best-of-five series tied one game apiece.
He noted the danger of reading too far into small playoff sample sizes this early in the postseason.
Still, he said there were things he was “thinking through” and “possibly kind of some changes” that could be enacted on Tuesday.
One possibility: Inserting Miguel Rojas and/or Kiké Hernández into lineup, perhaps in place of Max Muncy and/or Tommy Edman, to give the Dodgers extra right-handed bats against a dominant left-hander in Sale.
Another, more notable potential option: Moving Ohtani even further down the order from his current No. 2 spot, after he went just 2-for-8 in the first two games of the NLDS while continuing to battle right arm and left knee injuries.
“[We already moved] him from 1 to 2 –– but going further than that? I’m open to it,” Roberts said. “It’s something that, if I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why.”
The explanation, of course, wouldn’t be too complicated.
In Ohtani’s currently diminished physical state, he has simply not been the same presence at the top of the order that the Dodgers have grown accustomed to from the four-time MVP.
“Like we’ve talked about, he’s not 100%,” Roberts said.
But also, “I think there’s a little bit of [him also] trying to do too much,” Roberts added. “I think that’s a piece.”
Indeed, Ohtani has suffered from a futile combination so far in the playoffs, failing to either punish pitches over the plate or keep from chasing out of the strike zone.
“It’s hard to have success when you’re out of the zone,” Roberts said. “So I think that’s the thing, then the question is: How do we get him [attacking pitches back] into it?”
A change of mindset could help, especially against a premium pitcher like Sale (who has held Ohtani to a 3-for-15 mark with five strikeouts and only one double in their career head-to-head matchups).
“Trying to chase slug tomorrow night might not be the right plan, given the starter,” Roberts said.
Instead, Roberts pointed to the opposite-field single Ohtani slapped past a shift for his lone hit in Sunday’s Game 2 loss.
“That at-bat yesterday, the block base hit the other way, that’s something that is production,” Roberts said. “I think that’s something where, against a guy like Chris Sale, it gives you a chance.”
The Dodgers, of course, would love to get more pop from Ohtani, who led the team with eight home runs during last year’s World Series trek. Roberts also knows the slugger “feels the responsibility” to provide such power, which might be contributing to his lack of plate discipline.
Thus, for now, taking the pressure off Ohtani’s shoulders by potentially hitting him lower in the lineup might also prove to be prudent.
“At the end of the day, every conversation I’ve had with him is whatever’s best for the team,” Roberts said. “And he’s all in on [that]. I know that undoubtedly.”
While Roberts will contemplate other changes beyond Ohtani’s spot in the order, there were a few ideas he outright struck down Monday night.
The big one: Removing Andy Pages from the batting order despite his 0-for-7 start in the playoffs –– one that has felt reminiscent of his historic struggles last October, and been further marred by a consequential ABS challenge he missed in Game 1.
While Roberts said he feels Pages has been “trying to do too much” –– downplaying any lingering effects from the fractured hand that sidelined the center fielder for most of September –– he also said he wanted to give the 25-year-old slugger more leash.
“I believe in him,” Roberts said. “And I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re gonna need him to be an active part of our team.”
That was all part of the balance Roberts was trying to strike with his team’s season potentially hanging in the balance. It might still feel early for drastic changes. But one more loss, and the club’s three-peat bid will be on the brink.
“Our guys are our guys,” Roberts said. “Yeah, I can tweak a lineup. I can kind of insert, take out a player or two. But at the end of the day, we still have got to go out there and play and execute and take good at-bats.”

MILWAUKEE -- Los Angeles Dodgers utilitymanKiké Hernandezis expected to be activated in time to make his season debut Monday after recovering from surgery on his left elbow.
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said Sunday that Hernández should be available for the start of their home series against the Colorado Rockies.
"There's a different energy with Kiké," Roberts said Sunday. "There's a levity. There's an intensity. There's a good worker in there, a winning player. So I'm looking forward to having that edge."
Hernández, 34, signed a one-year, $4.5 million contract in February that kept him with the Dodgers. He underwent surgery last fall that kept him from playing for Puerto Rico in the World Baseball Classic and delayed the start of his 2026 season.
He hit .214 with a .298 on-base percentage with three RBIs in 12 games while on a rehabilitation assignment with Oklahoma City. He batted .203 with a .255 on-base percentage, 10 homers and 35 RBIs in 92 games with Los Angeles last season.
Hernández often has done his best work in October while helping the Dodgers win World Series in 2020, 2024 and 2025. He has batted .272 with an .826 OPS, 16 homers and 42 RBIs in 103 postseason games.
His return comes while Dodgers third baseman Max Muncy recovers after a 95.5 mph sinker from Milwaukee's Aaron Ashby hit him in the right wrist on Friday. X-rays were negative and the Dodgers expressed optimism that Muncy avoided a major injury.
"We were resolved to not having him available this weekend," Roberts said. "My expectation is that he's getting a little bit better today and maybe swing a bat tomorrow to see. I don't expect him in the lineup tomorrow either."
Muncy is batting .258 with a .363 on-base percentage, .515 slugging percentage, 12 homers and 19 RBIs in 48 games.

LOS ANGELES -- The Dodgers placed super-utility man Enrique Hernandez on the injured list Wednesday and will do the same with left fielderTeoscar Hernandez the next time they play Friday.
Enrique Hernandez suffered what Dodgers manager Dave Roberts described as a "significant tear" in his oblique earlier this week, an injury that will keep him out for several weeks, if not months. Teoscar Hernandez pulled up lame while running to first base in Wednesday's second inning and was diagnosed with a left hamstring strain, though the initial expectation is that his injury is not as serious.
"He tested well," Roberts said after the Dodgers' 4-1 win over the Colorado Rockies. "But we're going to get a scan tomorrow. Obviously it's an IL. There's just no timeline. But something like that obviously is going to be a few weeks at the minimum."
Enrique Hernandez spent the season's first two months building back up after offseason elbow surgery and suffered the oblique injury while taking batting practice before his season debut Monday. He picked up two hits that night, received treatment Tuesday, homered, then hit a fourth-inning double under significant pain in his left side and was later replaced on defense.
Cameras caught Roberts consoling a visibly shaken Enrique Hernandez in the dugout shortly thereafter.
"I feel pretty defeated right now," Hernandez told reporters after the game.
The Dodgers recalled infield prospect Alex Freeland to fill the vacant roster spot, starting him at second base for the series finale. Freeland will probably get most of the playing time there until Tommy Edman makes his expected return from offseason ankle surgery at some point in June, though Hyeseong Kim will draw starts at second base, too.
The hope is that Enrique Hernandez will at least return for the stretch run of the regular season so he can be a factor in the playoffs, the time of year in which he usually shines. Teoscar Hernandez's stay should be shorter, though it's nonetheless painful for the Dodgers, given his 1.018 OPS over the past 18 games.
"It's pretty frustrating for us," Dodgers center fielder Andy Pages said in Spanish. "We have the opportunity to see them work hard every day and prepare so that those things don't happen. But [injuries are] going to happen all the time."

Now that the 2026 MLB regular season is done, Sony made one last ratings tweak for many of the players across the league on October 2. The October MLB The Show 26 ratings update saw Mookie Betts & Cade Smith rise to join the other Diamonds in the game.
The notable changes
Mookie Betts is back as a Diamond in MLB The Show 26. He and Cade Smith were the only two to move to Diamond status on October 2. Betts moved to 85 OVR after a strong final few weeks. Over his last 14 games, Betts slashed .316/.418/.632 with four home runs and 10 extra-base hits.
Smith, meanwhile, notched 41 saves and struck out 107 batters over 74 innings this season for the Guardians.
Fernando Tatis Jr. moved up three points between the last update and now. Tatis Jr., before the start of the playoffs, hit five home runs and nine extra-base hits in the last 15 games of the regular season for San Diego.
Elly De La Cruz, who had eight extra-base hits in the final two weeks, moved to 87 OVR, a +2 OVR increase. He moved there, along with NL Wild Card hero Michael Harris II.
As for who went down, Yandy Diaz and Jacob deGrom were both downgraded from Diamond status.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA.
One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered.
Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula called upon
Catchers (2): Will Smith, Hunter Feduccia
For some reason, the Dodgers decided to carry three catchers on their Wild Card and NLDS rosters last year — Smith, Dalton Rushing, and Ben Rortvedt — but adjusted ahead of the NLCS by shedding Rushing, who received just one at-bat in the NLDS but otherwise rode the bench.
Rortvedt didn't get a start or even substitution after Game 2 of the NLDS with Smith slowly coming back from injury at the beginning of the postseason. Feduccia figures to play a similar break-glass-in-case-of-emergency role. As a lefty, he could get a start and then an early pull depending on matchups but, barring disaster, it's mostly going to be Smith's show.
Designated hitters (2): Shohei Ohtani, Josue De Paula
The Dodgers clearly want to find a way to bring De Paula with them in October, even if only as a lingering threat on their bench. They're reportedly not entertaining putting him in the outfield at all, and it's not hard to see why. Even if they're confident they'll be able to fix his defense in time, they can't afford any leakage in the postseason.
Ohtani is still shaking off the cobwebs from his 15-day IL stint. He picked up a few hits with promising exit velocity in his return against the San Diego Padres and later against the San Francisco Giants, but there are still question marks around what version of him we might see this postseason.
Infielders (6): Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, Tommy Edman, Max Muncy, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández
A notable exclusion here is Hyeseong Kim. Although he's in the running to get a spot on the bench and exclusively come into games to pinch-run or for reassurances on defense, there's still a chance he doesn't make the roster if the Dodgers are set on carrying 13 pitchers. Edman and Hernández, though lacking the same speed as Kim, can still offer the same defensive versatility.
Outfielders (3): Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández
Pages might've found himself in the same boat as Ohtani, but he announced his return to the Dodgers after a month-long IL stint in a big way, hitting .333 with a 1.180 OPS, two homers, and five RBI against the Padres and Giants. No doubt Dave Roberts and Andrew Friedman breathed a massive sigh of relief.
Alex Call will be the odd man out. He was on all four of LA's playoff rosters last year and received sporadic appearances throughout the month, but that was when Michael Conforto was still on the payroll. Tucker and Hernández have certainly had their ups-and-downs this season, but the Dodgers would never seriously consider leaving them out.
Starters (4): Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal, Tyler Glasnow
There's not much to say about what's probably the best rotation going into the postseason. Snell and Glasnow have both battled injury this season but came back when the Dodgers needed them most. It might be too much to ask that any of Yamamoto, Snell, or Glasnow replicate their dominance from last year, but they'll certainly try.
Relievers: (9): Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Justin Wrobleski, Edwin Díaz, Kris Bubic, Edgardo Henriquez
Just like 2025, this is where things get dicey. The Dodgers' bullpen isn't quite as banged up or as unreliable as they were last year, but they're not the air-tight, bulletproof coterie that their combined salaries suggest they should be. Henriquez will be coming straight off of the IL to rejoin the team in the NLDS, and Díaz, Sasaki, and Scott are all woefully unpredictable.
There is some thought that the Dodgers might carry eight relievers instead of nine, to free up a spot on the position player side for a guy like Kim. In this scenario, we'll stick with them taking nine. If not, Bubic is the most obvious cut. Last one in, first one out.

For nine-plus innings, the Dodgers and Giants couldn’t buy a hit with a runner in scoring position, but in the tenth, the Dodgers broke through for a 5-1 win. Alex Call and Andy Pages recorded two-out hits, a double, and a three-run shot to give the Dodgers their first lead in this game and the only one they’d need.
Dodgers find their breakthrough in extras to beat the Giants
Making a habit out of squandering chances through nine innings, the Dodgers scored four in extras to beat the Giants
Before getting to that point of being tied in extras, Jack Dreyer did a reasonable job of keeping the Giants at bay as an opener, but a stolen base allowed the opportunity for just a pair of singles to open the scoring in the second. Shay Whitcomb singled and stole second, later driven in by Scott Bandura—his first RBI of the season, playing in just his 13th big league game. Bandura also tried to steal a base, but this time Dreyer was alert to the danger and picked him off.
Facing a traditional bullpen game with Carson Seymour completing just one inning to open this one, the Dodgers first threatened to score in the third, the inning marked by Tony Vitello’s ejection. With two on and a 2-2 count to Mookie Betts, a check swing in which he probably went around was called a no-swing. Vitello came out to argue what had already been a topic of frustration earlier in the game and was thrown out for the seventh time in his 2026. The Giants, however, got out of the jam, as Betts struck out on the next pitch, and Sam Hentges also punched out Freddie Freeman.
What the Dodgers offense couldn’t do in the third, it did in the following frame. Kyle Tucker got on to leadoff the inning thanks to a defensive error by the second baseman and moved to third on a Max Muncy double—his 27th of the season, setting a new career high in a single season. With two on and one out, Andy Pages evened the score with a sacrifice fly.
Through the following innings, the Dodgers kept threatening but never coming through, first with a Freddie Freeman hit with a man on being taken away by a great defensive play from Jonah Cox—somewhat redeeming himself for the error that contributed to the Dodgers’ first run. That, by the way, would be Freeman’s last action in the game, replaced after five by Kiké Hernández as Dave Roberts rotated key pieces.
In the sixth, Muncy nearly wrote another chapter in his book as a giant killer. But the deepest part of the park was just deep enough to keep him from a solo shot in a ball that would’ve gone out in 23 of 30 stadiums. Perhaps the biggest squandered chance, though, came in the seventh and eighth when the Dodgers first stranded a leadoff double by Tommy Edman with three straight groundouts—an inning later, after Muncy secured his third hit of the day, Andy Pages hit into an inning-ending double play with two on and one out.
The Dodgers’ pitching was the reason the offense kept getting these opportunities to take the lead. Justin Wrobleski was the first pitcher out of the bullpen for the Dodgers, but looking for an even distribution of workload, he only completed two scoreless innings in under 30 pitches. Roki Sasaki and Edwin Díaz combined to strike out three, each with a scoreless frame.
Although Wrobleski had a couple of scares, the Giants truly came back to threaten again in the seventh when Bobby Miller took the mound, but also without actually breaking through. With runners at the corners and no outs, Miller secured a strikeout, then lucked into Marcelo Mayer staying at third on a wild pitch quickly recovered by Hunter Feduccia, recorded another punchout, and finished off the inning with a groundout.
With both teams exhausting new ways of threatening without actually scoring, the Giants looked like they’d take the lead with a leadoff bomb in the eighth by Christian Koss. However, the call on the field of a home run was overturned when replay made it clear it was a foul ball, and the score remained 1-1 through nine innings.
Even in the tenth, it looked like the Dodgers were going to strand the ghost runner after their first two hitters were retired without him advancing to third, but Call came through, and an intentional walk later, Pages had the big hit of the game. With the four RBI he recorded in this game, Pages left Ohtani behind and isolated himself as the Dodgers’ RBI leader this season, with 85.
Sunday particulars
Home run: Andy Pages (23)
WP —Alex Vesia (3-1): 1 IP, 1 hit, 1 strikeout
LP —Duncan Davitt (0-1):1 IP, 2 hits, 4 runs, 3 earned runs, 1 walk
Up next
The Dodgers get a little under a week off before they get back on the field on Saturday at home. They’ll be playing host to the winner of the Wild Card round between the Braves and Phillies in game 1 of the NLDS. No starters have been announced for that series.

item.content:encoded:
Freddie Freeman is back where the Los Angeles Dodgers like him: in the middle of a loaded order, on the last afternoon of the regular season.
After sitting Saturday against the San Francisco Giants, the Dodgers first baseman is in Sunday’s Game 162 lineup at Oracle Park and batting third.
The card posted by Underdog MLB puts Shohei Ohtani at designated hitter, Mookie Betts at shortstop, Freeman at first, Kyle Tucker in right, Teoscar Hernández in left, Max Muncy at third, Andy Pages in center, Hunter Feduccia behind the plate and Tommy Edman at second. Jack Dreyer is listed as the starter in what figures to be a bullpen game.
The off day was not a surprise. Freeman had started each of the previous 10 games and was dragging a .522 OPS over 45 plate appearances in that stretch.
Enrique Hernández filled in at first on Saturday while the club gave its 37-year-old cornerstone a breather.
That is how Dave Roberts has handled September: keep Freeman available, not exhausted, with the postseason a few days away.
Sunday’s assignment is the one Freeman has occupied for most of his career.
He has started more than 1,300 games in the three-hole across Atlanta and Los Angeles, and even after spring talk about a cleanup role behind Tucker, the Dodgers keep sliding him back between Betts and the middle of the order when they want their most reliable left-handed bat seeing traffic.
He entered the weekend hitting .290 with 167 hits, 16 homers and 70 RBIs. The power has been quieter lately — he has gone without an extra-base hit for more than two weeks — but the bat-to-ball skill is still the reason Los Angeles trusts him with runners on.
The context around the lineup is October-minded. Los Angeles is 99-62 and chasing a 100-win season in the finale. Will Smith is the only everyday starter sitting.
Blake Treinen is headed to the injured list with a shoulder issue, so the bullpen will be asked to work. First pitch is 12:05 p.m. PT / 3:05 p.m. ET on SportsNet LA.
For Freeman, the message is simple. One rest day. Then back in the three-hole, glove at first, with Ohtani and Betts in front of him and Tucker behind him.
If the Dodgers are going to finish 100-62 and carry momentum into the NLDS, they want their veteran first baseman in the middle of it — not on the bench, and not buried in the order.
Sunday is a tune-up with meaning: one more look at the group that has to win in October.

SAN FRANCISCO -- When Blake Snell took the mound for the final time in the regular season on Saturday afternoon, he eased any lingering concerns the Dodgers may have had after the southpaw exited his previous start with left groin tightness.
The Dodgers wanted to see Snell make close to a full start in order to feel good about him taking the ball going forward, but they weren't going to push him. So Snell's outing was finished after he had thrown four innings on 77 pitches (50 strikes), allowing one run on five hits while striking out three Giants.
The Dodgers had initially hoped to have Snell pitch five innings, but he was not at his sharpest, having thrown only one inning in the past two weeks due to his groin issue. But it was better to brush the rust off now than in the postseason.
"Really encouraged by it, and just happy to get my legs underneath and get going and completely move past the groin," Snell said. "I mean, it felt great today, and the velo was good. And was inconsistent -- I’ve got to figure my body out a little more, but I got a week to do so, and I'm really looking forward to that."
Limited to only nine regular-season starts by left shoulder fatigue, loose bodies in his left elbow and the groin issue, Snell is not only determined to get back to where he was last postseason, when he recorded a 3.18 ERA through six outings (five starts). He wants to continue to grow.
"I want to be better than what I was last October. I think I can definitely do that," Snell said. "But we all need each other. I think that's the biggest thing."
Snell's status had been the primary concern surrounding L.A.'s daunting four-man postseason rotation that also features Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Tarik Skubal and Tyler Glasnow. Now that Snell has made his final regular-season tuneup, the main question for the Dodgers is how to line up their starting four for the NL Division Series, which begins on Oct. 3 at Dodger Stadium.
"I think as a pitching staff, we're going to be OK," said Kiké Hernández, who hit a game-winning solo homer in the top of the ninth inning. "So it's up to the offense to do what we're capable of doing."
There is a compelling case for each of those four starters to be the ace in any given rotation in the Majors. The Dodgers feel good about any of them making a Game 1 start, so the decision essentially comes down to how they can get the most out of their starting four.
"To be honest with you," Roberts said, "you could put them all in a hat, and you could make a case for any order you put them in."
One consideration is rest. The Dodgers ran a six-man rotation for most of this season, meaning their starters are accustomed to five days' rest. Yamamoto has not started a game on less rest than that -- although he did pitch on back-to-back days to clinch MVP honors in last year's World Series. Skubal, Snell and Glasnow all have experience pitching on four days' rest.
Here's what that could mean for the NLDS, when the Dodgers can reset their rotation to their liking: Yamamoto starting Game 1 would allow him to start a potential Game 5 on his usual rest. Skubal, Snell or Glasnow could start Game 2, then be available for a potential Game 5 on four days' rest.
It may also be on the table for whoever does not start Games 1 and 2 to be available out of the 'pen, like in last year's NLDS, when Glasnow pitched 1 2/3 innings in relief in the series opener before starting Game 4.
The aim for the Dodgers, Roberts said, is to "maximize those four guys," who are the strength of their pitching staff.
"We're only as good as our starters," Snell said. "And I love our starters, I love the staff, the way we push for each other to be great and support each other. … It's what we've all been waiting for, and now it's time to prove it. It's an important time for us."

27 Sep 2026, 21:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Darren Yamashita)
The Los Angeles Dodgers will look to tarnish the final game of longtime San Francisco Giants broadcaster Mike Krukow's career with a 100th regular-season win when the California rivals wrap up the regular season on Sunday afternoon.
The finale in San Francisco will send the Dodgers (99-62) on their quest for a third consecutive World Series championship and Krukow into retirement after 36 years of calling Giants games.
Also a pitcher for the Giants for the final seven of his 14 seasons in the majors, Krukow, 74, will be honored after Sunday's game, in which the home team will seek to end a four-game losing streak overall and a seven-game skid against the Dodgers.
'I'm going to tell them just how much they mean to me and my family,' Krukow promised this week about his farewell speech. 'I don't know if you can convey it in words, but it'll be conveyed in emotion. That I can guarantee.'
Krukow was in the booth when San Francisco won three World Series titles in five seasons from 2010-14, but the team has been to the postseason just twice since then (2016, 2021), losing both times in the National League Division Series. This season, the Giants (65-96) will finish with their fewest wins in a full season since going 64-98 in 2017.
Meanwhile, the Dodgers will wind up with more wins than the 98 they had in 2024 and 93 last season, regular seasons followed by World Series victories. This will be their 14th consecutive appearance in the postseason; they also won the World Series in the pandemic-shortened season in 2020.
With a first-round bye to start their three-peat effort as a result of having the second-best record in the National League, the Dodgers will need 11 wins to achieve a first in Major League Baseball since the Yankees captured the World Series in 1998, 1999 and 2000.
Los Angeles saw a lot go right in its first two games in San Francisco -- both victories -- as they got home runs from Teoscar Hernandez, Andy Pages, Enrique Hernandez and Mookie Betts, sharp starting pitching from Tarik Skubal and Blake Snell, and stellar game-closing from Tanner Scott.
The Dodgers will take the field Sunday with postseason roster spots still up for grabs and pitchers needing one more outing before a five-day break leading into a best-of-five NLDS, which will open in Los Angeles on Saturday.
'We want to finish playing good baseball,' Dodgers manager Dave Roberts told reporters. 'Our guys still got to get ready because we've got a week of not playing baseball. So (the goal is) just to finish strong, finish the season out.'
One unresolved issue for Los Angeles in the postseason is who will bat leadoff.
Shohei Ohtani, who manned the spot almost exclusively while healthy earlier in the season, led off Friday's 2-0 win over the Giants, going 0-for-4 with three strikeouts.
Roberts moved Betts into the top spot for Saturday's 4-3 victory, and while Betts went just 1-for-5 with a strikeout, his hit was his 23rd home run of the season.
Ohtani, who singled and struck out twice while slotted second on Saturday, has gone just 4-for-18 with just one extra-base hit, a double, since returning from a 16-day absence due to discomfort in his right biceps.
While the Dodgers have not announced a starting pitcher for Sunday's game, the Giants will send right-hander Carson Seymour (0-2, 4.70 ERA) to the mound as an opener. He will make his first start after 24 relief appearances this season.
Seymour does not have a decision in five career outings against the Dodgers. He has a 3.60 ERA, allowing two runs in five innings. He pitched the sixth inning on Saturday, striking out one.
--Field Level Media
